annotations.text:
Lido, redrawn for iOS 26.

White ground throughout. Colour arrives as soft blurred light rather than as fills — 60–80px blurred discs sampled from the trip cover, sitting behind the white so the glass has something to refract. Nothing on the page is a flat tinted panel.

Chrome is Liquid Glass and floats: nav is a set of capsules rather than a bar, and the composer and dock sit above content that visibly passes under them. Two variants, used consistently — regular glass over content, clear glass only over a cover with a scrim beneath it.

Type is Geist for the interface (SF-adjacent, tight tracking at display sizes) and Newsreader Light for trip and place names.

The structural move underneath: a trip's four tabs (Overview / Packing / To-Do / Food) become one scrollable trip page with module cards, so outstanding work is visible without hunting.

The kit

Every value here is lifted from the screens: hairlines are 0.5px of ink at 7% rather than a grey fill, cards carry a hairline plus a wide soft shadow, and glass always gets an inset top specular highlight so it reads as a lens rather than frosted plastic.

On photos — Unsplash is blocked by this session's network policy (403 on images.unsplash.com, unsplash.com and plus.unsplash.com), and the artifact CSP blocks external images regardless, so a photo has to be embedded rather than linked. Trip covers are drawn instead. Give me image files and I will inline them; the layouts take a photo unchanged.

Two directions I did not take, sketched so you can push back. These are pre-glass wireframes — they are about structure, not surface.

Option B treats the trip as an operations board — fastest to answer "what do I owe the group?", but it reads like a task app. Option C treats it as a loose board of cards you arrange — feels like the holiday, but it is hard to scan and expensive to build. The Screens page sits between them, leaning toward B's clarity with C's warmth.
